transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Priya N. (Redwood), Danielle Park (Citrine), Ravi Kapoor (Citrine), Marta Alvarez (Citrine)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics — streaming, key params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p), retry/backoff strategy, and where caching/batching helps. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for initial pilot; security and data retention questions came up. Agreed next steps: send pricing & SOC2/security docs, share SDK sample with streaming and retry best practices, schedule poc scoping.

Topics:
- Overview of Redwood Hosted API
- Streaming responses and chunking behavior
- Generation params and deterministic tuning
- Retries and idempotency for streaming requests
- Cost/latency tradeoffs, caching hints
- Security/compliance notes (SOC 2, KMS)

Transcript:
[00:00] Olivia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Olivia with Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our SE. How's it going?
[00:08] Danielle: Hey Olivia, thanks. Doing good. We have about 40 minutes, hope that's OK. Marta and Ravi are here as well.
[00:13] Marcus: Yep perfect. We'll keep it focused. Quick agenda: show hosted API basics for chat and text gen, demo streaming, talk about params, and close with next steps.
[00:24] Marta: Sounds good, we want to understand what the hosted path gives vs self-hosting, and also what controls we have for latency and cost.
[00:33] Olivia: Great, that's exactly what we'll hit. Danielle, can you remind us what you're prototyping?
[00:38] Danielle: Sure — we're building an assistive search chat for our support docs. Expecting ~1000 qps during peak for the chat front-end across multiple regions, but initial pilot is much smaller. Key is short latencies (<250ms) for single-turn responses and deterministic quality for templates. Also security — our data is internal.
[00:53] Ravi: And we need SSO + audit logs, and KMS integration for keys.
[00:58] Olivia: Great. We'll start with a quick demo. Marcus, over to you.
[01:03] Marcus: Cool. I'm going to share my screen.
[01:08] [screen share noise]
[01:12] Marcus: So first the simple call — this is our hosted REST API. You POST messages, system/user/assistant roles, model param, and some generation params. Example: { model: "redwood-1" , messages: [...], max_tokens: 128, temperature: 0.2 } — obviously in the demo I'll use a smaller prompt.
[01:30] Danielle: Quick clarification: does the API accept streaming? We need partial tokens for UI.
[01:35] Marcus: Yes — streaming is supported via server-sent events and websocket options. If you enable streaming=true we emit tokens as they're generated. The SDK has helpers to reassemble.
[01:46] Marta: How do retries work with streaming? If the connection drops mid-stream, can you resume?
[01:52] Marcus: Good question — currently we don't support true byte-range resume. If a stream disconnects, best practice is to perform a client-side reconciliation: you keep the tokens received, then retry the request with a dedupe/idempotency key and a stream starting from the full prompt; Redwood will try to return the same output if model/params unchanged but small nondeterminism possible. We show a pattern where you send a message_id + request_id and on retry we use request_id to detect duplicates.
[02:17] Ravi: So no native resume, but idempotency + client reconciliation. That fits. Any guidance on retry backoff?
[02:23] Marcus: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 retries for transient network errors, and treat 5xx as retryable only if short lived. For streaming we typically rewind and resend the full request. We'll share sample SDK code.
[02:36] Danielle: Good — can you show how params like temperature/top_p affect output, especially determinism?
[02:41] Marcus: Absolutely. Lower temperature (0—0.3) plus top_p narrow the sampling and increase determinism. If you need templated/responsive answers we often recommend temperature 0.0—0.2 and setting max_tokens appropriate. For true deterministic output you can use deterministic mode with beam or n best—though note exact deterministic bit-for-bit is tricky across model versions.
[03:03] Marta: You mentioned model versions — how do we pin versions and rollouts?
[03:07] Olivia: On hosted we let you pin a model version in the call or at the account/route level; we also have rollout controls so you can canary a new model to X% traffic. The console shows token-level latency/cost and you can set fallbacks.
[03:19] [05:00 marker skipped for brevity, conversation continues]
[05:04] Marcus: Here's a streaming example — I'm going to query a short support prompt. You can see tokens arriving chunked every ~50ms.
[05:12] Olivia: In the stream the SDK attaches partial role frames, so frontends can render incrementally. Also, to reduce flicker we provide 'delta' events that group tokens.
[05:23] Danielle: Nice. Is there guidance on chunk size and UI jitter?
[05:27] Marcus: UX best practice: render after 40—80ms of idle or after N tokens to avoid jitter. We'll share our sample component.
[05:34] Ravi: On cost — streaming vs non-streaming shouldn't change token pricing right?
[05:38] Olivia: Correct — billing is token-based (input+output). Streaming only affects latency/UX. The unit economics are driven by token count, model choice, and whether caching/prefix caching can cut repeated context.
[05:50] Marcus: That brings up caching — for chat you can prefix-cache common system messages or reuse KV cache between requests with dedupable prefixes; hosted has automatic prefix caching for repeated prompts within a session to save compute.
[06:04] Marta: That would help with our FAQ templates — many prompts share the same instructions.
[06:08] Olivia: Exactly.
[06:10] Danielle: On params: what about max_tokens and truncation? We have variable-length context and sometimes we hit limits.
[06:16] Marcus: We provide length-aware truncation strategies: head, tail, sliding window. For chat it's common to keep recent messages and compress older context with summarization. We also expose token_count in responses so you can instrument and alert.
[06:30] Ravi: Any guidance on rate limiting and throttling for hosted? We want graceful degradation.
[06:35] Olivia: Hosted has per-account quotas and burst configs. For client-facing apps we recommend client-side rate limiters and fallback to cached answers or a lower-cost model. Redwood routes by policy and will fallback to a cheaper compatible variant if you configure that.
[06:49] Marcus: I'll show the console rules — you can set policy: prefer low-latency region, fallback-to-model-x, and set per-route qps.
[06:57] [console demo noises]
[07:02] Danielle: Security time: data retention and encryption?
[07:06] Olivia: Hosted keeps raw logs for X days by default — we have enterprise options for log retention and can configure no-retention or customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). SOC 2 and ISO docs are available; we'll share those.
[07:19] Marta: Can we bring our own VPC or is that only for Private?
[07:23] Marcus: Private deployments support VPC and on-prem; hosted doesn't require VPC. For hosted enterprise we offer private networking peering options in some regions.
[07:33] Ravi: Does hosted allow SSO and RBAC?
[07:36] Olivia: Yes SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC in the console. Audit logs are available as an add-on.
[07:44] Danielle: Back to retries: if we dedupe with request_id, are there any edge cases with partial successes?
[07:50] Marcus: The main edge case is nondeterministic sampling; if the model produces different tokens on retry you'll need to reconcile. For high consistency you can lower temperature and use deterministic sampling; also log request_id and returned hashes to detect mismatches.
[08:07] Marta: Any limits on request size for streaming vs non-streaming?
[08:11] Marcus: The limits are the same — token limit per model; streaming doesn't change that. Very long contexts will be truncated.
[08:18] Olivia: We'll also share guidance on splitting multi-turn into multiple short requests to reduce token re-processing.
[08:24] [10:00 marker skip]
[10:10] Marcus: Quick note on retries for idempotent calls: for non-streaming small responses you can use a request_id and server-side dedupe semantics. For streaming we recommend client reconcile and tie UI to the request lifecycle.
[10:26] Danielle: Okay — you mentioned SDK samples and code. What languages?
[10:30] Marcus: JS/TS, Python, and an official socket/websocket helper for streaming. We'll attach examples for React and Node.
[10:37] Ravi: For performance testing — can we run a quick benchmark? We need p99 latency numbers on our sample prompt.
[10:42] Olivia: Absolutely — pilot typically includes a small benchmark run. We can run a perf test using your sample payloads; Marcus can coordinate.
[10:48] Marcus: We'll need sample queries and expected concurrency; we'll provide a script that hits the hosted endpoint with warmup and measures p50/p95/p99.
[10:56] Danielle: Good. On pricing, are there commit tiers for hosted?
[10:59] Olivia: Hosted is usage-based with volume discounts; we also offer committed reserved capacity for predictable throughput (Dedicated). For pilot you can start hosted and then move to Dedicated as qps grows — Redwood supports that migration path.
[11:13] Marta: Is there a SLA on hosted?
[11:16] Olivia: Hosted has a baseline SLA for enterprise tiers; Dedicated has stronger latency/uptime guarantees. We'll share our SLA doc.
[11:23] [15:00 marker skip]
[15:12] Marcus: Demoing retry sample code now — here's a simple JS snippet: try request, on error if transient then await backoff and retry with same request_id, for streaming capture tokens into buffer and on final chunk validate.
[15:28] [code noise]
[15:31] Danielle: That looks straightforward. How do we monitor per-route cost?
[15:36] Olivia: In the console you can break down by route/model/token type; we also export usage to your billing or to a CSV.
[15:43] Ravi: Any recommendations for model selection for short answers?
[15:47] Marcus: Use a smaller, low-latency model for short factual answers and reserve larger models for complex reasoning. Redwood's catalog has verified perf profiles so you can pick based on latency/cost/quality.
[15:58] Danielle: Can we test with our documents for retrieval-augmented generation?
[16:02] Marcus: Yes — RAG is common. We recommend embeddings+vector store and issuing short prompts with top-k retrieved context. Hosted supports embedding endpoints and integration tips.
[16:12] Marta: Regarding data residency — our EU region requirement means data cannot leave EU. Hosted can route regionally; Private if strict.
[16:20] Olivia: Correct, we can route to EU regions and configure residency, but if you need isolated on-prem that is Private.
[16:28] Ravi: Ok final logistics: timeline is pilot in 4—6 weeks?
[16:33] Danielle: Yes, pilot in April would be ideal.
[16:36] Olivia: Great. To recap next steps — we'll send pricing/pilot doc, SOC 2/security, SDK sample for streaming/retries, and a perf script. Marcus will coordinate the benchmark once you share payloads.
[16:49] Marta: Perfect.
[17:00] Olivia: Any final questions?
[17:03] Danielle: One small one — what about partial token dedupe on our side? If we show partial result and then retry, UI could duplicate. Any suggested UI pattern?
[17:12] Marcus: Show the request_id and mark partials as provisional; on a retry replace provisional block with finalized result. Keep an append-only log of token blocks with IDs.
[17:23] Ravi: That makes sense.
[17:26] Olivia: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll follow up by Friday with the docs.
[17:31] Danielle: Thanks all.
[17:33] Marta: Thanks.
[17:35] [call ends]
